content: The Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Prevention, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Care for Key Populations, updated in July 2016, provide comprehensive recommendations for addressing HIV among vulnerable groups. These guidelines emphasize the importance of prevention strategies, including condom use, male circumcision, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and access to clean needles. Despite these efforts, the global HIV epidemic persists, with 2.3 million people living with HIV and 3 million new infections reported in 2013. This highlights the urgent need for additional safe and effective prevention methods. Men who have sex with men (MSM) bear a disproportionate burden of HIV in many countries, even in regions with generalized epidemics. Although effective HIV prevention interventions exist for MSM, access to these services is often hindered by political, structural, and social barriers, including stigma and marginalization. PrEP involves the use of antiretroviral drugs by HIV-negative individuals to prevent infection. Over the past decade, five major clinical trials have evaluated the effectiveness of PrEP among various populations, including people who inject drugs, serodiscordant couples, heterosexual women, and high-risk MSM. The iPrEx study, conducted across six countries, was the only trial specifically focused on MSM. It showed a 44% reduction in HIV transmission in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, with efficacy increasing to 73% among participants who adhered to the regimen on 90% or more days. Resistance to the drug was rare and limited to participants with undetected acute HIV infection at baseline. Safety concerns were minimal, and both study arms reported increased condom use and reduced numbers of sexual partners. In 2012, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed guidelines recommending PrEP for serodiscordant couples, MSM, and transgender individuals at high risk of HIV. These guidelines have since been updated to reflect new evidence, focusing on oral PrEP containing tenofovir (TDF). A systematic review examined whether oral PrEP should be used for HIV prevention among MSM, considering outcomes such as HIV infection rates, adverse events, condom use, and changes in the number of sexual partners. The review included randomized controlled trials published between 1990 and 2014, with no restrictions on location or language. The iPrEx trial, a Phase III randomized controlled trial, evaluated the safety and efficacy of daily oral FTC-TDF (emtricitabine and tenofovir) compared to placebo among 2,499 MSM across six countries. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 67, with 1% identifying as female. The study demonstrated a 44% reduction in HIV risk, with higher efficacy among those with better adherence. Adverse events were similar between the intervention and control groups, and there was no significant difference in the number of sexual partners or condom use between groups. Awareness of PrEP among MSM has increased since the release of the iPrEx results, but it remains limited globally. Willingness to use PrEP varies widely, with most studies reporting acceptance rates between 40% and 70%. Barriers to PrEP use include concerns about effectiveness, side effects, cost, accessibility, stigma, and mistrust of healthcare providers. Facilitators include perceived effectiveness and support from healthcare providers. Studies also highlight the importance of addressing issues such as criminalization, discrimination, and violence against MSM during PrEP implementation. Cost-effectiveness analyses of PrEP among MSM have been conducted primarily in the United States, Australia, and Peru. Results vary depending on factors such as PrEP efficacy, cost, HIV incidence, and program prioritization. In the U.S. and Australia, estimates range from cost-saving to over $300,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) saved. In Peru, PrEP is considered cost-effective at $1,702–$2,755 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) saved, below the WHO-recommended threshold for cost-effective interventions in the region. Healthcare providers generally support PrEP but report barriers to its real-world implementation, including concerns about antiretroviral resistance, adherence, and the lack of local guidelines. Provider awareness of PrEP is high, but prescribing practices remain limited.
